stem:
Litware, Inc. builds a support chatbot in Python that calls the Messages API. When a user asks a follow-up question, Claude answers as if the conversation had just started. The application currently sends only the newest user message in each request.

What should the developer change?
choices: Add a cache_control marker to the newest user message so that the API remembers the earlier turns
Set stream to true so that the connection keeps the conversation state open between questions
Send the earlier user and assistant turns together with the new message in the messages array of every request
Increase max_tokens so that the response has room to refer back to the earlier turns
explanation: The Messages API is stateless, so the application must send the full conversation history, including earlier assistant turns, with each request. Prompt caching only lowers the cost of a repeated prefix; the prefix still has to be sent. Streaming changes how a response is delivered and max_tokens only caps its length, so neither gives the model any memory of earlier turns.

stem:
Adatum Corporation extracts invoice fields with the Messages API. The code ends the messages array with a prefilled assistant turn that contains an opening brace so that Claude starts a JSON object. After the team moves to a newer Claude model that no longer accepts prefilled assistant turns, requests return HTTP 400. The downstream parser requires output that is guaranteed to follow a fixed schema.

What should the developer do?
choices: Remove the prefill and use structured outputs to constrain the response to the JSON schema
Remove the trailing whitespace from the prefilled assistant text and resend the request
Remove the prefill and ask in the system prompt for a reply that contains just the JSON object
Keep the prefill and add a stop sequence that matches the closing brace of the object
explanation: Models that do not accept a prefill return a 400 error, so the prefill must be removed. Because the output must follow a schema, structured outputs are the documented replacement, since they constrain the response to the schema. A system prompt instruction does not guarantee how the response starts or that it matches a schema, the whitespace rule applies only to models that still accept a prefill, and a stop sequence does not remove the rejected turn.

stem:
Wingtip Toys adds a chat assistant to its web store. The assistant calls the Messages API without streaming, so shoppers see a blank panel until the whole answer is ready. The team wants the answer to appear word by word while Claude generates it.

Which change should the developer make?
choices: Move the requests to the Message Batches API and poll for the finished answer
Set stream to true and render the text of each text_delta event as it arrives
Add cache_control to the system prompt so that the answer is returned from the cache
Lower max_tokens so that each request returns before the shopper notices a delay
explanation: Setting stream to true returns server-sent events, and the generated text arrives in content_block_delta events whose delta type is text_delta, which the UI can render immediately. The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously and returns results later, so it does not suit an interactive chat. Prompt caching reduces the cost of repeated input and a lower max_tokens only truncates the answer; neither makes partial text available early.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. streams Claude responses to a web client. During a busy period, some streams end with an overloaded_error event even though the API had already returned HTTP 200. The current code checks only the HTTP status when the stream opens, so users see half-finished answers and no error.

Which two actions should the developer take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Treat the 200 status returned when the stream opened as proof that the whole response succeeded
Handle errors that surface while the stream is being read, because an error can arrive after a 200 status
Discard the partial text, because content received before an error cannot be reused in a later request
Capture the partial response received before the failure and use it to build a continuation request
Send the same request again with stream set to false, because a non-streaming request cannot return an overloaded_error
explanation: An error can occur after the API returns 200, and the SDK surfaces it as an exception to the code that reads the stream, so that code must handle it. Keeping the partial response lets the application send a continuation request instead of reprocessing everything; tool_use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered. Trusting the initial status misses mid-stream errors, discarding partial text wastes recoverable work, and non-streaming requests can also return an overloaded error as HTTP 529.

stem:
Northwind Traders sends scanned receipts, stored as JPEG files on a private file server, to Claude through the Messages API on the Claude API. Each request must be self-contained: the team wants neither a separate upload call nor a tool round trip before Claude can see an image, and the files are not reachable from the internet.

Which approach should the developer use?
choices: Image content blocks with a url source that points to the file server
Image content blocks with a file source that references a file_id from the Files API
A client tool that reads the file and returns it in a tool_result block
Image content blocks with a base64 source and the image/jpeg media type
explanation: A base64 image source embeds the image bytes in the request, so it works for private files in a single self-contained call. A url source needs an image the API can reach, a file source needs an earlier Files API upload, and a client tool adds an extra round trip before Claude can see the image.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. runs an agent on the Claude API that works through many screenshots in one long conversation. Each request resends the full history and the screenshots are base64 encoded, so request size and latency grow with every turn. The screenshots are generated at run time and must not be exposed on a public URL.

What should the developer do?
choices: Upload each screenshot once through the Files API and reference it by file_id in later requests
Switch the image blocks to url sources that point to a public storage location
Set stream to true so that the screenshots are sent to the API in smaller chunks
Move the conversation to the Message Batches API so that the batch stores the history
explanation: Each request resends the history, so base64 images are included in the payload on every turn; uploading once and referencing a file_id keeps payloads small however many images accumulate. A url source would also shrink the payload, but it needs a publicly reachable image, which the screenshots must not have. Streaming changes response delivery, not request size, and the Batches API is for asynchronous bulk work rather than an interactive agent.

stem:
Relecloud's research assistant uses extended thinking in manual mode on a model that supports it. The request sets budget_tokens to 10000 and max_tokens to 8000, and the request fails validation. The team still wants a large thinking budget.

What should the developer change?
choices: Lower budget_tokens to 512 so that it fits inside max_tokens
Set display to omitted so that thinking tokens stop counting toward max_tokens
Raise max_tokens above budget_tokens so that the final answer still has room after thinking
Switch the request to streaming so that the budget is no longer limited by max_tokens
explanation: In manual mode thinking tokens count toward max_tokens, so budget_tokens must be less than max_tokens; raising max_tokens leaves room for the answer. A budget below the 1,024-token minimum is rejected, display only controls whether thinking text is returned (billing and limits are unchanged), and streaming does not change the rule.

stem:
Tailspin Toys runs an agent loop on the Messages API with extended thinking enabled. When Claude returns a tool_use block, the code copies only the text and tool_use blocks of the assistant message into the next request, appends the tool_result, and drops the thinking blocks to reduce request size. The team wants Claude's reasoning to stay intact across the tool call.

How should the developer build the follow-up request?
choices: Include a summary of the dropped thinking in the system prompt of the follow-up request
Keep the thinking text but remove the signature field to reduce the request size
Pass every thinking block back unmodified with its tool_use block, followed by the tool_result
Drop the thinking blocks and rely on the model to regenerate its reasoning from the tool_result
explanation: When tool results are returned, the thinking blocks of the assistant message must be passed back complete and unmodified, because the server uses the signature to reconstruct the original thinking and the tool result continues one reasoning flow. A summary in the system prompt, a block without its signature, or no thinking block at all each break that continuity.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. writes a Python service that calls Claude directly on the Claude API with the Anthropic SDK. The company does not use Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud for this workload.

Which credential should the service use to authenticate?
choices: A Claude API key from the Claude Console, sent in the x-api-key header
Temporary AWS credentials that sign each request with SigV4
Google Cloud Application Default Credentials for an identity that can call Vertex AI
An Amazon Bedrock API key passed as a bearer token
explanation: The Claude API authenticates with an API key; the SDK reads it from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and sends it in the x-api-key header together with the anthropic-version header. SigV4 signing and Bedrock bearer tokens belong to Amazon Bedrock, and Application Default Credentials belong to Google Cloud.

stem:
Litware, Inc. hosts its workloads on AWS. A Python service must call Claude through the InvokeModel API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint by using Anthropic's SDK with AWS credentials from the default credential chain.

Which client class should the developer instantiate?
choices: AnthropicBedrockMantle
AnthropicAWS
AnthropicBedrock
AnthropicVertex
explanation: AnthropicBedrock is the client for InvokeModel on the bedrock-runtime endpoint and resolves AWS credentials through the default chain. AnthropicBedrockMantle targets the separate bedrock-mantle endpoint, AnthropicAWS is for Claude Platform on AWS, which Anthropic operates, and AnthropicVertex is for Google Cloud.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. develops on laptops and calls Claude through Google Vertex AI by using the AnthropicVertex client in Python. The client is created with a project ID and a region, but requests fail with an authentication error.

Which credentials should the developer configure?
choices: A Claude Console API key in the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable
AWS access keys in the AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY variables
A Bedrock API key in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable
Google Cloud Application Default Credentials for an identity that has permission to call Vertex AI
explanation: The AnthropicVertex client authenticates with Google Cloud credentials, for example Application Default Credentials created with gcloud auth application-default login, for an identity whose role includes the aiplatform.endpoints.predict permission. A Console API key is for the Claude API, and the AWS keys and the Bedrock key are credentials for Amazon Bedrock.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank runs the same Python code against several platforms. For a Haiku-tier model released before the 4.6 generation, the model ID on the Claude API is claude-haiku-4-5-20251001. The code now targets Google Vertex AI through the AnthropicVertex client.

Which model ID should the developer pass?
choices: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
claude-haiku-4-5@20251001
anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0
us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0
explanation: On Vertex AI, models earlier than the 4.6 generation use the Claude API ID with an at sign in place of the hyphen before the snapshot date. The unchanged Claude API ID is the form for the Claude API, and the last two choices are the Amazon Bedrock base model ID and its US inference profile ID.

stem:
Tailspin Toys calls an older Claude model on Amazon Bedrock through InvokeModel. A request that passes the base model ID anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 fails with HTTP 400 and a message that on-demand throughput is not supported and an inference profile is required. Company policy requires that inference traffic stays inside the United States geography.

Which model ID should the application pass?
choices: global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0
eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0
us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0
claude-sonnet-4-5@20250929
explanation: Models that AWS serves through cross-region inference need an inference profile ID, which is the base model ID with a prefix. The us. prefix keeps routing inside the United States geography. The global. prefix routes dynamically across regions, the eu. prefix routes inside Europe, and claude-sonnet-4-5@20250929 is the Vertex AI form of the ID.

stem:
Alpine Ski House calls Claude on Google Vertex AI with plain HTTPS requests instead of the Anthropic SDK. The team adapts a working Claude API request.

Which two changes should the team make to the request? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Name the model in the endpoint URL and leave the model field out of the request body
Keep sending the Claude Console API key in the x-api-key header
Keep sending the anthropic-version header with the latest API version
Set anthropic_version in the request body
Request streaming by adding stream set to true to the body of the same endpoint
explanation: A Vertex AI request differs from a Claude API request in two main ways: the endpoint URL names the model, so the body omits it, and anthropic_version goes in the body rather than in a header. The request authenticates with Google Cloud credentials rather than a Console API key, and streaming uses the separate :streamRawPredict endpoint instead of a stream field.

stem:
Lucerne Publishing has a Python service that sends product photos to Claude on the Claude API by using url image sources. The service must now call Claude on Amazon Bedrock, and requests that contain url image sources fail. The photos stay in a private Amazon S3 bucket.

What should the developer change to keep vision working?
choices: Replace the S3 object URL with a pre-signed URL in the url image source
Read each photo, base64 encode it, and send it as a base64 image source
Upload the photos with the Files API and reference each file_id
Submit the image requests through the Message Batches API instead
explanation: Amazon Bedrock accepts only base64 image sources, so the application must encode the images itself and stay within the per-image and request size limits. URL image sources, including pre-signed URLs, the Files API, and the Message Batches API are listed as not supported on Bedrock.

stem:
Margie's Travel runs a Python service on AWS compute that has an IAM role attached, and the service can sign requests with AWS credentials. Security guidance asks for the most preferred authentication method for calling Claude on Amazon Bedrock.

Which method should the service use?
choices: A long-term Amazon Bedrock API key stored in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK variable
A short-term Amazon Bedrock API key generated in the console and copied into configuration
A Claude Console API key sent in the x-api-key header
Temporary credentials from the IAM role, used to sign requests through the default AWS credential chain
explanation: AWS recommends signing requests with temporary AWS credentials whenever possible, so bearer tokens, which AWS calls Amazon Bedrock API keys, are the least preferred path and fit software that cannot sign requests. This service can sign, so the IAM role credentials fit. A Claude Console API key authenticates to the Claude API, not to Amazon Bedrock.

stem:
Relecloud's batch job calls the Claude API over HTTPS from Python. Some requests return HTTP 429 with a rate_limit_error and a retry-after header. The job retries immediately in a tight loop and keeps failing.

What should the developer do?
choices: Wait for the interval in the retry-after header, then retry with exponential backoff and a retry limit
Treat the 429 like a 400 invalid_request_error and correct the request body before retrying
Switch the same requests to streaming so that the rate limit no longer applies
Reduce the request timeout so that failed requests are retried sooner
explanation: A 429 is a rate limit response, so the client should honor the retry-after header and back off, with a limit on retries because some 429 responses persist until access resumes. A 400 means the request itself is malformed, streaming does not bypass rate limits, and a shorter timeout does not change how often the limit is hit.

stem:
Trey Research enables extended thinking and tools on a Messages API call in Python. The code reads the reply with json.loads(message.content[0].text) and raises an AttributeError on some responses, because the first block is sometimes a thinking block.

What should the developer do?
choices: Read message.content[-1].text, because the text block is the last block of a response
Read message.content[1].text, because a thinking block occupies the first position
Loop over message.content, select the block whose type is text, and parse its text value
Parse message.to_json(), which contains just the generated text of the reply
explanation: The content of a response is a list of typed blocks, so code should select blocks by type instead of by position: a text block can follow a thinking block and can be followed by a tool_use block. Position-based reads break when the block order changes, and to_json() serializes the whole message rather than the text alone.

stem:
Wide World Importers exposes an asyncio-based Python web service that calls Claude. The service uses the synchronous Anthropic client, so each call blocks the event loop and concurrent requests queue up.

Which change should the developer make?
choices: Set stream to true on the synchronous client so that the call returns immediately
Create an AsyncAnthropic client and await client.messages.create in the request handlers
Submit each prompt through the Message Batches API and poll for the result
Raise max_retries on the synchronous client so that blocked calls are retried
explanation: The SDK provides AsyncAnthropic with the same interface as the synchronous client, and awaiting its calls lets the event loop serve other requests. Streaming on the synchronous client still blocks the calling thread, the Batches API is for asynchronous bulk work with delayed results, and retries do not make a call non-blocking.

stem:
Lamna Healthcare Company generates long reports with the Python SDK. A non-streaming request with a very large max_tokens raises a ValueError because it is expected to take longer than about 10 minutes. Some corporate networks drop idle connections. The downstream code needs the complete Message object and does not display partial text.

How should the developer call the API?
choices: Override the timeout option with a larger value so that the check no longer raises
Increase max_retries so that the SDK repeats the slow request until it finishes
Switch to AsyncAnthropic so that the request is no longer subject to the timeout check
Use client.messages.stream and call get_final_message to obtain the complete Message
explanation: For long-running requests the SDK recommends streaming, and its accumulation helper get_final_message returns the same complete Message that a non-streaming call would, while the open event stream keeps the connection from looking idle. A larger timeout only disables the check and leaves the idle-connection risk, more retries repeat the same slow request, and the async client has the same timeout behavior.

stem:
Coho Winery adds the anthropics/claude-code-action GitHub Action to its repository so that developers can mention @claude in pull requests. The workflow file is committed to the repository.

Which two actions should the team take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Store the API key as a GitHub Actions secret and reference it in the workflow as a secrets value
Put the API key in the env block of the committed .claude/settings.json file
Add the API key to the CLAUDE.md file so that Claude can authenticate on each run
Let Claude push its commits directly to the default branch to keep the history linear
Review the changes that Claude proposes in a pull request before they are merged
explanation: Claude Code GitHub Actions guidance is to keep credentials in GitHub secrets, never in committed files, and to review Claude's changes before merging. The settings.json and CLAUDE.md files are committed to version control, so a key placed there is exposed, and pushing directly to the default branch skips the code review that protects it.

stem:
Southridge Video hosts its code on GitHub and has a Claude Team plan. Leadership wants every pull request reviewed by Claude automatically, with inline comments, and does not want engineers to write or maintain workflow files for it.

Which option should the team use?
choices: A GitHub Actions workflow that runs claude-code-action with a review prompt
Code Review, turned on by an organization Owner through the Claude GitHub App
The /code-review command, run by each developer on a local branch
A custom reviewer subagent that developers invoke during a Claude Code session
explanation: Code Review is a managed service that reviews pull requests on GitHub according to repository settings and posts inline comments, so nobody maintains a workflow. A GitHub Actions review runs in your own CI from a workflow file you maintain, /code-review runs only when a developer invokes it locally, and a custom subagent is invoked by a person or by Claude during a session.

stem:
Fourth Coffee uses Code Review on its GitHub repositories. Reviews report only correctness bugs, but the team also wants missing tests flagged. A developer adds a REVIEW.md file with that guidance to a feature branch and opens a pull request, but the review ignores it.

What should the team do?
choices: Raise the review level to Deep so that the review also covers missing tests
Merge REVIEW.md into the default branch, because the review reads it from the base or default branch
Choose a different review model in the Code Review admin settings
Rename REVIEW.md to CLAUDE.local.md on the feature branch
explanation: Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch and never from the changes of the pull request being reviewed, so the guidance takes effect after it is merged there. The review level sets how thorough a review is rather than what it flags, the admin settings do not offer a model choice, and CLAUDE.local.md is a personal file that is not committed.

stem:
Humongous Insurance keeps a CLAUDE.md at the root of its monorepo that tells Claude Code to indent with tabs. The packages/api folder has its own CLAUDE.md that says to indent with spaces. Developers start Claude Code in packages/api and report that the indentation Claude uses is inconsistent.

What should the team do?
choices: Remove the contradiction so that one indentation rule remains across the CLAUDE.md files that load
Rely on the CLAUDE.md in packages/api, because it replaces the root file for sessions in that folder
Move the root instructions into CLAUDE.local.md so that they rank lower than the nested file
Add an @import of the root file to the nested file so that the nested rule wins
explanation: Claude Code loads the CLAUDE.md files from the working directory and every directory above it and concatenates them, so a nested file does not replace its parent, and contradictory instructions may be followed arbitrarily. The fix is to review the files and remove the conflict. CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md and an import only adds more text to the context, so neither settles a conflict.

stem:
VanArsdel, Ltd. has a 600-line project CLAUDE.md. Claude Code follows its rules less reliably, and most of the frontend rules are irrelevant when developers work on backend code. The team wants to cut the context cost of the file without losing the frontend rules.

What should the team do?
choices: Split the file into topic files and import each one into CLAUDE.md with @path syntax
Move the frontend rules into CLAUDE.local.md at the project root
Move the frontend rules into files under .claude/rules/ that declare a paths field for the frontend folders
Move the frontend rules into the managed policy CLAUDE.md file
explanation: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ load only when Claude works with matching files, so backend sessions do not pay for the frontend rules. Imports are expanded and loaded together with the CLAUDE.md that imports them, so they organize a long file without reducing its context cost. CLAUDE.local.md and the managed policy CLAUDE.md both load in every session.

stem:
Graphic Design Institute shares its Claude Code configuration with every developer through the Git repository. Each developer also keeps personal preferences for this project, such as sandbox URLs and a personal model override.

Which two files should the team keep out of version control? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: CLAUDE.md at the project root
CLAUDE.local.md at the project root
.claude/settings.json
.claude/settings.local.json
.claude/rules/testing.md
explanation: CLAUDE.local.md holds personal, project-specific instructions and should be added to .gitignore, and .claude/settings.local.json holds personal project settings and overrides, which Claude Code keeps out of git when it creates the file. CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, and the files under .claude/rules/ are the team-shared project configuration and belong in the repository.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank requires that Claude Code does not read .env files on any developer machine. A permissions deny rule for these files must stay in force even if developers edit any settings file in their repository or home folder, or pass --settings at startup.

Which location should the security team use to define the deny rule?
choices: In the shared .claude/settings.json file committed to each repository
In the user ~/.claude/settings.json file on each developer machine
In the project CLAUDE.md file as an instruction that forbids reading .env files
In managed settings delivered by the organization
explanation: Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order, and nothing in a developer's own settings files or in --settings overrides a managed key. The shared project file and the user file are files that developers can edit, and a CLAUDE.md instruction is guidance for Claude rather than an enforced permission rule.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. runs Claude Code against the Claude API. Developers select the opus alias in settings.json. After a Claude Code update, the alias resolves to a newer Opus model and the team sees different behavior in its prompts. The team wants the opus alias to stay on the model it has validated.

What should the team do?
choices: Set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to the validated model so that requests are routed to it
Set ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL to the full name of the validated model
Run /model default so that the session reverts to a fixed runtime model
Keep the model value as opus in settings.json and commit the file to share the alias
explanation: Aliases point to the recommended version and update over time; to pin one, use the full model name or set the matching environment variable such as ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL. ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL changes where requests go, not which model answers, the default value only clears an override and returns to the runtime default, and committing the alias still lets it move.

stem:
Munson's Pickles and Preserves Farm will roll out Claude Code to many developers through Amazon Bedrock. Without configuration, Claude Code resolves aliases such as opus and sonnet to built-in defaults for the provider. That default can lag the newest release, and the model it names may not yet be enabled in a developer's AWS account. The administrator wants to control exactly when users move to a new model.

What should the administrator do before the rollout?
choices: Set ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL and the matching Sonnet and Haiku variables to version-specific Bedrock model IDs
Set availableModels in managed settings to the opus, sonnet, and haiku aliases
Set the model value in managed settings to an alias such as opus so that every user starts on it
Set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to the regional Bedrock endpoint for the AWS account
explanation: On third-party providers the documentation advises pinning model versions before rollout by setting the ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL variables to version-specific IDs in the provider's format, and then updating them when the organization chooses to move. An allowlist of aliases only restricts selection, an alias in the model setting still resolves to the built-in default, and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL changes the destination of requests, not the model.

stem:
Northwind Traders publishes a Claude Code plugin named deploy-kit that calls an MCP tool provided by another plugin, audit-logger. A new audit-logger release renamed that tool and broke deploy-kit for everyone who updated. The team wants deploy-kit to receive only compatible 2.1 patch releases of audit-logger.

How should the team declare the dependency?
choices: In the dependencies array of plugin.json, as the plain string audit-logger
In enabledPlugins of the committed .claude/settings.json file, with the entry audit-logger set to true
In the dependencies array of plugin.json, as an object with name audit-logger and a version range of ~2.1.0
In the project CLAUDE.md file, with an instruction to use audit-logger version 2.1
explanation: A plugin declares dependencies in the dependencies array of its plugin.json, and an object entry can carry a semantic-version range such as ~2.1.0 so that only matching releases are installed. A bare string follows whatever version the marketplace provides, enabledPlugins turns plugins on without constraining versions, and CLAUDE.md is instruction text that does not control installation.

stem:
Adventure Works Cycles maintains the secrets-vault plugin in its own Git repository. Another team's plugin declares a dependency on secrets-vault with the version range ~2.1.0. Installing that plugin fails with a message that secrets-vault has no git tag satisfying the range, although the plugin.json of secrets-vault shows version 2.1.0.

What should the maintainer of secrets-vault do?
choices: Add allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn to the marketplace.json file of the root marketplace
Create the release tag secrets-vault--v2.1.0 on the commit, for example with claude plugin tag --push
Run claude plugin prune on every machine that installs the dependent plugin
Change the version in plugin.json to 2.1.0-0 so that the range accepts pre-release builds
explanation: A version constraint resolves against git tags named plugin-name--v-version on the repository that hosts the plugin, so the maintainer must tag each release; the version field in plugin.json alone does not satisfy the range. The cross-marketplace allowlist solves a different problem, claude plugin prune removes auto-installed dependencies that nothing needs, and a pre-release version would not match the range.
